Finding a variable

The search box on the home page matches names first, then labels and question text. Each release (and table) has a page listing its variables; each group, such as a battery of questions with a shared stem, has a page listing its members; and each pair of adjacent releases has a page of what was added, removed or changed. A variable that was renamed has one page, under its latest name; its earlier names lead there.

Reading a variable page

SectionWhat it holds
Label and factsthe label, the release (and table), storage type, measure and units, and the publisher's page for the variable
Universewho was asked, as the publisher states it, by week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024) when it changed
Questionthe question text, verbatim; each wording, with the week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024)s, forms or modes it applies to
Codeseach code with its label, its kind, its missing types, and what classified it ("Classified by"); Cases, where the codebook counts them
Valid rangethe range of valid values, for numeric variables
Availabilitywhich week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024)s (and forms) have the variable; see below
Code historythe publisher's history of a variable's codes, where it gives one
Correctionserrors in the publisher's documentation this repository corrects: the original, the correction, the evidence, and whether it was reported to the publisher. Corrected fields are marked corrected
Groupsthe groups the variable belongs to
Releasesthe variable in each release, and what differs from the latest one; see below
Other linkslinks to variables it was built from, split from or merged into
Topicsannotations, for finding variables; not facts about the data
Provenancewhere the record, and each field that came from elsewhere, came from

Where each fact came from

Every fact has an origin, shown in grey next to it or in the Provenance table. Source facts, corrections and derived facts stay apart.

OriginMeaningIn this repository
publisherread from the publisher's documentation5,196
upstream_packageread from a third-party package that redistributes the publisher's documentation (gssrdoc)0
data_fileread from the data file's own metadata: Stata or SPSS labels, extended missing values4
rulecomputed by a named rule from other fields1,417
handa judgment entered through a hand-written build input, by a person or an agent. author names who made it: a person, or the agent and the work it was doing ("Claude (PublicDataToolkit Task 35)", naming the task in the toolkit's planning files), never a person who didn't make or check it2,536
modeldrafted by an LLM0

Codes and missing values

Codes are stored as they appear in the data file. Each has a kind:

KindMeaningCodes here
validan answer or value, as the publisher classifies it4,017
missinga missing-value code, with one or more missing types saying why1,339
unresolveda code the sources don't explain; never recoded by missing type unless asked0

A missing code has one or more missing types, which say why the value is missing, so the data can be recoded by type (don't know one way, not applicable another) instead of collapsing every missing code into one null.

Missing typeMeaningExamplesCodes here
dkThe respondent didn't know or couldn't chooseGSS .d; ANES 98 "DK"0
refusedThe respondent refusedGSS .r0
no_answerNo answer recorded, reason unknownGSS .n; ANES 99 "NA"640
inapNot applicable: outside the universe or skipped by designGSS .i "iap"0
skippedThe respondent skipped it (self-administered modes)GSS .s "skipped on web"683
not_askedNot asked of this respondent's wave, form or interview, including a panel round the respondent missedGSS .y "not available in this year"; ANES "no Post IW"; NLSY -5 "non-interview"0
not_availableAsked, but not released in this fileGSS .x "not available in this release"0
uncodeableAnswered, but couldn't be coded or imputedGSS .u, .p0
unknownThe source records the value as unknown. For administrative and coded data, where no respondent was askedFARS "Unknown", "Reported as Unknown"0
unspecifiedThe source marks the code missing but gives no reasonGSS .z "see codebook"16
otherAnything else; say what in the label0

Releases, links and lineages

A link joins a variable in one release to a variable in another and says how they relate. Links record continuity the publisher asserts, or that a named rule found, never an equivalence guessed from names. A variable's page covers its whole history: releases joined by links that keep the meaning form a span, and a link that changes the meaning (codes, wording, universe or range) starts a new span, with the change and its evidence shown between them.

RelationMeaningLinks here
same_itemThe same question, asked the same way1,427
renamedThe name changed0
wording_changedThe question text changed17
codes_changedThe value set changed55
range_changedThe valid range or a top code moved while every code kept its meaning (Pulse TBIRTH_YEAR's yearly top code; THHLD_NUMPER 1–10 → 1–40)5
labels_changedThe variable label or value labels changed (e.g. a corrected label). When the codes changed too, the link also lists codes_changed8
universe_changedWho was asked changed0
data_revisedThe same item, but its values in the data were revised between releases: recoded missing codes, restored or corrected data, reassigned cases. Release notes are the usual source0
derived_fromfrom is built from to, as a cumulative-file variable is built from single-year items0
split_fromOne variable became several, or several became one0
merged_intoOne variable became several, or several became one0
rescaledThe same construct, but the scale was re-estimated, so values aren't comparable across the pair without the publisher's trend or linking file. PISA's ESCS and BELONG are re-estimated each cycle0

Availability

The Availability table on a variable page has a row for each week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024) and a column for each form (or other dimension) that had the variable. A cell gives the number of non-missing responses when known, or ✓. A week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024) inside the variable's span that didn't have it reads "not in this week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024)". Here, a week (2020-2023) or cycle (2024) is: Each week or cycle is one release, so a release holds one wave, named like the release (week01-week63, cycle01-cycle09). Every release is `current`: each is a different wave, not a superseded version of another.

Complete and approximate results

The agent views and pdt search label every result by how it was produced, not by how confident anyone is in it:

LabelThe result isAllowed in the filter
completeevery record in scope that matches the filter, with nothing elseonly fields whose origin is publisher, upstream_package, data_file or hand, and groups with those origins
complete_by_rulethe same, but the filter also uses derived properties or rule-made groupsthe above, plus derived properties and origin: rule groups, each with its rule version
approximateanything else: text search, annotations, or a result an agent assembled itselfanything

Getting the data

The publisher's terms let the common-format files be shared. Build them from the publisher's files:

make download ARGS=--accept-terms   # the publisher's files, after reading their terms
make data                           # data/processed/*.parquet, checked cell by cell

One file per release and table, such as data/processed/pulse-cycle09-puf.parquet. Each variable has a value column with the valid answers, and, when it has missing or unresolved codes, a <name>__code column holding the code, as text, wherever the value is missing. So a missing code never looks like an answer, and nothing the publisher recorded is lost: pdt.data.rebuild puts the publisher's codes back. pdt.common_format has the file names and code texts.

In Python, pdt.extract.extract(".", release, [names], missing={...}) writes an extract, recoding each missing type as you say.

Using the records from Python

The records are JSONL, one record per line, in metadata/releases/<release>/[<table>/]variables.jsonl, with groups.jsonl, links.jsonl and corrections.jsonl beside them. Anything can read them. The PublicDataToolkit library applies the corrections and answers labeled searches:

from pdt.check import Repo
from pdt.search import Index, search

repo = Repo.load(".")
index = Index.from_repo(repo)          # records, corrections applied
result = search(index, {"name": "NAME"})   # a filter as data
print(result.to_dict())                  # matches, with their completeness label

From the command line: pdt search . --filter '{"text": "depression"}', and pdt check . to check the repository against the standard.

Using the agent views with an LLM

Give the model agent/SKILL.md first: it says how to use the shards and how to label answers. agent/index.md describes the dataset and lists the shards, each small enough to read whole, by release, group and subject, in two forms: JSONL, and one line per variable. Every shard says how complete it is, and an answer built from it should say so too. The full records in metadata/ stay canonical.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Household Pulse Survey public use files, 2020-2024. This product is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.
